title: AI System Design: From Idea to Production - Apoorva Joshi, MongoDB

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk presents a developer-focused four-phase framework for designing AI systems from idea to production, serving as methodology and tooling for engineers building AI applications. The framework is general-purpose but uses a health insurance claims review system as the running example, grounding it in healthcare and enterprise operations. The four phases cover product requirements, system design, evaluation and monitoring, and optimization for production. Prerequisites include general AI/ML familiarity and basic understanding of LLMs and retrieval systems. This is a conference presentation by Apoorva Joshi (MongoDB) at the AI Engineer channel. summary: Apoorva Joshi opens by arguing that vibe coding—shipping AI-generated code without specification—is dangerous for production systems, citing Anthropic and OpenAI leaders who emphasize that specs and system design now matter more than code. She introduces a four-phase framework: product requirements, system design, evaluation and monitoring, and optimization for cost, latency, and reliability. The framework is applied to a health insurance claims review system for MDB Health, where medical reviewers currently spend two days processing claims—four times the industry standard for non-urgent cases and twelve times for urgent ones. The product requirements phase involves quantifying the business problem in a user-specific, measurable, solution-agnostic way; gathering business constraints such as data residency, approved vendors, and mandatory human review for complex cases and denials; identifying AI's role along three dimensions (critical vs. complementary, reactive vs. proactive, autonomy level); and defining SMART success metrics, such as reducing urgent claim processing time from two days to one hour within ninety days of launch. The system design phase covers data strategy—identifying needed data sources, storage formats, update frequencies, and processing requirements—and matching retrieval techniques to data types. For architecture, Joshi surveys common AI design patterns (RAG, AI agents, agentic systems, control flows, LLM as router, human-in-the-loop, fine-tuning) and selects RAG for retrieval, control flow for the pre-structured workflow, and human-in-the-loop for reviewer escalation, while advising to start simple and iterate. She then covers end-user experience design—input forms, approval or denial output with citations, embedding in MDB Health's website, feedback via reviewer overrides and flagged citations—and technology stack decisions constrained by earlier product requirements. The evaluation and monitoring phase introduces guardrails for invalid inputs and hallucinated outputs, alongside metrics for guardrail compliance (claim rejection rate, missing citation rate), response quality (faithfulness), domain-specific accuracy (claim processing time as North Star), and system health (cost per recommendation). Production monitoring adds implicit success indicators like human override rate and review duration. Finally, optimization techniques address accuracy (prompt engineering, reranking, memory), cost and latency (semantic caching, batch processing), and reliability (structured outputs). Joshi closes by emphasizing that evaluation must be built in from the start—'you can't improve what you can't measure'—and points to MongoDB's GenAI cookbook for examples of retrieval techniques, agentic design patterns, and evaluation and optimization techniques.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.summary: Apoorva introduces herself and argues that vibe coding is dangerous for production systems; specs and system design are now the critical skills.

sections.title: Framework Overview
sections.summary: Introduces a four-phase framework: product requirements, system design, evaluation and monitoring, and optimization for cost, latency, and reliability.

sections.title: Use Case: Health Insurance Claims Review
sections.summary: Introduces the real-world example of a health insurance claims review system to simplify the manual adjudication process for medical reviewers.

sections.title: Product Requirements: Business Problem and Constraints
sections.summary: Covers quantifying the business problem in a specific, measurable, solution-agnostic way and gathering business constraints including data residency, approved vendors, human review requirements, and performance requirements.

sections.title: Product Requirements: Role of AI and Success Metrics
sections.summary: Discusses identifying AI's role along three dimensions (criticality, reactivity, autonomy) and defining SMART success metrics aligned with the business problem.

sections.title: Data Strategy
sections.summary: Covers identifying data sources, storage formats, update frequencies, and processing requirements including chunking, embedding, metadata extraction, and PII removal.

sections.title: Retrieval Techniques and System Architecture
sections.summary: Matches retrieval techniques to data types and maps the claim flow through the system, advising to start simple and iterate rather than over-engineering with agents.

sections.title: AI Design Patterns and Selection
sections.summary: Surveys common AI design patterns (RAG, agents, agentic systems, control flows, LLM as router, human-in-the-loop, fine-tuning) and selects RAG for retrieval, control flow for the structured workflow, and human-in-the-loop for reviewer escalation in the claims system.

sections.title: End User Experience and Feedback Design
sections.summary: Covers UX questions including system input and output, deployment location, triggers, human role, self-explanation via citations, and feedback mechanisms through reviewer overrides and flagged irrelevant citations.

sections.title: Technology Stack Decisions
sections.summary: Discusses selecting models, data processing tools, embedding models, vector databases, and orchestration frameworks, noting that constraints from product requirements should guide these decisions.

sections.title: Evaluation: Guardrails and Metrics
sections.summary: Introduces guardrails for probabilistic LLM systems—input guardrails to reject invalid/irrelevant inputs and output guardrails to detect hallucinated or uncited responses—along with metrics for guardrail compliance, response quality (faithfulness), domain-specific accuracy (claim processing time as North Star), and system health (cost per recommendation).

sections.title: Production Monitoring
sections.summary: Covers monitoring production for regressions by tracking offline evaluation metrics plus implicit success indicators like human reviewer override rate and time to review AI recommendations.

sections.title: Optimization for Production
sections.summary: Discusses optimization techniques for accuracy (prompt engineering, reranking, memory), cost and latency (semantic caching, batch processing), and reliability (structured outputs) needed before moving to production.

sections.title: Final Takeaways and Closing
sections.summary: Closes with key takeaways: think deeply about product requirements before coding, identify constraints early since they shape downstream decisions, design the simplest system that meets your needs then iterate, and build evaluation in from the start. References MongoDB's GenAI cookbook for examples of retrieval techniques, agentic design patterns, and evaluation and optimization techniques.

limitations: AI cannot fully automate all cases—human review required for complex cases and denials
Vector search may miss medical terminologies like diagnosis and procedure codes
System can be semi-autonomous at max due to business constraints
Guardrails needed because LLM-based systems are probabilistic and can produce unexpected, incorrect, or harmful outputs

Processing time is 4x industry standard for non-urgent cases

Clinical guidelines update annually, coverage policies quarterly, claims history hourly
